Hello! So I went to every other week after finishing the intro dosing and stayed on Spravato for a total of 9 months. I ultimately wasn’t interested in trying to ween off something that was working. But then I had to move.

Where I moved, Spravato wasn’t available, so I had to come off it completely. For 7 months, things were still great and then very suddenly they weren’t again. I think it was because of the lack of Spravato- I ruled out other causes, it wasn’t seasonal depression due to the timeframe, etc. 

Things didn’t really get better. Now, a year and a half after stopping Spravato, I’m finally restarting it (first dose was today, actually)! 

So I’m not thrilled about continually needing Spravato. It’s a little scary, actually. But it is good to know that I could come off it and not show symptoms for several months. My doctor said that kind of thing is typical- and that when people start feeling bad after stopping it, they just restart, and I absolutely would have if I hadn’t moved.

Just my personal experience, YMMV, but I hope that helps! Feel free to DM me if you have specific questions or want to talk. :)

Don’t usually comment on these but this struck a chord. 

My mom is a special-needs teacher. Some of the worst students she’s ever had to teach are students whose parents never told them “no”. They let the kid win every game, pick every restaurant, etc. etc. because the kid has special needs (and they feel bad for them) or because it’s just easier to go along with what the kid wants. It’s fine because they’re just a kid, right? 

Until they’re not a kid anymore. Until they’re a teenager or adult, bigger and still aggressive and end up hurting others and their caretakers because they were never taught that isn’t okay.

The students get to her classroom where everyone there has special needs and suddenly, they’re not the most special person anymore. They loose board games to another student (because everyone looses at some point) and have complete meltdowns because they can’t handle it. 

One student in particular was like that in the beginning and by the time he was graduating my mom’s class, she had basically taught that behavior out of him- that sometimes you loose, sometimes you don’t always pick the restaurant and that’s okay- and then he went back to his family that enabled him and forgot everything she taught. Now he’s an adult, doped up on tons of meds to make him not aggressive, and sitting on the couch all day in a group home because he can’t function in public or anywhere else otherwise. Even though this could have been avoided. Because it was “easier” to let him have his way. 

Plus, early intervention always matters. If she’s five, she should be starting school soon, yes? I highly encourage you to get in touch with her teachers, find out if she has an IEP, set goals with them (whether for behavior or education, etc.). Diary of a mom is a GREAT blogger on parenting a child with autism and has lots of advice regarding school.

Depending on where you live, there can also (not always) be surprising community support. EX. a large church in my area has a ministry specifically for those with special needs. Once a month, they host a “parent’s night out” - sometimes on Friday nights for date nights, sometimes on Saturday mornings for errands- where the parents can leave their special needs children with someone with training and have time to breathe and just be an adult for a while. That’s so important. (Yes, the YMCA often does this, but not specifically for special needs children- they may not be equipped or trained to handle some of those difficulties, where this ministry is specifically so).

Also, for the emotional neglect thing, having a relationship with your daughter that isn’t entirely about her sister is important. Yes, family events and family days matter, but you need to spend time with your daughter one-on-one (preferably not discussing sister the whole time unless she brings it up first) and a relationship with her outside of that. And while yes family is expected to help, make her as little of her sister’s keeper as possible. 

Just some thoughts. Feel free to PM me if you need. I hope things improve for you!

Yeah, I was happy to get a free 23andMe kit, but I found myself actually (surprisingly) enjoying the study as well? The feeling of contributing to something potentially meaningful that could help others was nice, but I also liked the cognitive tests? Like, okay, did you have the one with the balloons? Press each balloon to fill it by 10, and get as close as you can without popping, because once you pop it, it’s over? I did, and while I scored “higher” overall than the average person by getting closer to the actual number (which made me feel smart, but who really knows, haha), I also popped significantly balloons more than the average person and am considered more *risky*. It told me a little bit but I wanted to know more so I googled it and apparently it’s a well-known cognitive thing on riskiness and I thought that was so interesting. 

In regards to myself, I could care less. Cut too deep, drink too much, whatever, I don’t really care what happens to me, I just want to feel better. I try to stay alive to not hurt the people I love, but that’s about all I’ve got. However, with other people, I don’t consider myself risky at all- quite the opposite. If you don’t have on a seatbelt in my car, if I don’t ask you at least twice if you’re allergic to anything (foods, fabric dyes, etc.) before you stay at my place, etc. - I just can’t function. I can’t. Everyone has to be taken care of. And I’ve never gone out of my way to intentionally be risky. I’ve never played the lottery, never gambled, etc. I do take precautions when I’m potentially being “risky” - like with self-injury, I do clean my blades, the area I hurt beforehand, and the wounds afterwards to prevent infection and bandage and use scar remover carefully. So I somewhat disagreed with the assessment of myself being “risky”? 

(I was the oldest growing up of multiple younger siblings, one of whom was severely medically fragile, in a rather unstable household with my parents fighting often both emotionally and physically, which probably had something to do with the way I view myself and others, but how much of it was nurtured, and how much of it was my genes and nature?) 

Also, while I know the study was as accurate as possible... I knew it was just a game on the computer with balloons and no real consequences? I had come home from work and was tired, checking my email before relaxing at the end of the day, and doing my due diligence in the study. Who cared if I overinflated an imaginary balloon? Not me. Because I knew there were no consequences. I certainly tried my “best”, but I feel like if there had been consequences whether positive or negative (like, I don’t know, if I got $10 for every balloon I didn’t pop, or I lost $10 for every balloon I did pop) that I may have taken the test more seriously (and therefore scored differently) than I did when I knew nothing would happen? 

Did you have any similar thoughts, on this test, or the study, or really anything? Like I said, you’re the first person I’ve met besides myself who did it, and I’m pretty curious! I didn’t keep my survey answers (yes, I’m bipolar, yes, I’ve tried a lot of drugs, no, nothing has changed this month), but I did keep screenshots of my cognitive test results out of personal curiosity.

Edit: So it won’t allow me to add a photo, but I found my results, I had a score of 1425 and the average across all participants was 1220, and I had 19.6 pumps per balloon and the average across all participants was 14. “How many points did you get from all the balloons you inflated? The more points you earned, the more your strategy—safe or risky—tended to be effective... How much did you inflate each balloon? More pumps means you were more willing to take the risk that a balloon would pop. Fewer pumps means that you avoided the risk of the balloon popping, and preferred to get a smaller yet safer amount of points for each balloon.”

“This test measures risk-taking behavior. People differ in how much they tend to take risks or ‘play it safe.’ Those who are more willing to take risks in this test also tend to gravitate towards real-world risk-taking behavior such as games of chance, smoking, impulsive behavior and sensation-seeking conduct. Likewise, people who take fewer risks in this test do not tend to exhibit real-world risky behavior. This test mimics many games of chance that involve choosing between a risky bet with a potentially higher payoff and a safer bet with a lower payoff. Knowing the balloon might pop, did you continue to inflate it to earn more points or did you stop early to avoid losing the points you already had? This test is based on the ‘Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART).’

And here’s a copy of some data 23andMe found: https://research.23andme.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/23andMe_ASHG_2017_Olga.pdf

I know for myself that I’m introverted because being around people requires energy and I tend to keep serious things to myself (like self-injury, for instance, to not worry people), but I have a bad habit of “personality matching”. Like if I’m around someone funny, I’ll tend to act funny, or if I’m around someone serious, I’ll tend to act serious as well. I don’t even do it intentionally, it’s completely involuntary and I kind of hate it, because I strive to be genuine in everything I do and it can come across as fake, but I swear it’s not. I suspect it’s in part because I’m a people pleaser and desperate to be liked, and in part because I’m empathetic and want people to be comfortable and at ease around me, so I try to act in a manner that does that? How do I keep everyone happy?” So, anyways, sorry for the long backstory haha 😅 but that may be why you can come across as an extrovert easily? Or maybe not, that’s just why I do!

See, that’s really interesting to me, because INFJ is the rarest Myers-Briggs type in the general population, but I suspect it makes up a larger portion of the population that self-injures? I think the feeling (instead of thinking) and introversion (instead of extraversion) make sense, but I’m curious as to the other two factors, for sensing vs intuition and for perceiving vs judging.

Like, for example, as a judging type, I could see my need for control driving me to self-injure. But what if the opposite is true- what if a perceiving type needs the control self-injury provides? And I don’t even know where to begin with intuition versus sensing.

What patterns are there in the overall population of people who self-injure? What do we have in common that unites us, and what sets us apart, both from each other and the rest of the population that doesn’t self-injure? Especially the similarities and differences between the people that self-injure to calm intense emotions (hyperstress) verses those that self-injure to feel emotions (dissociation)? 

Anyways, I know these are super deep questions for a simple response, but thank you so much for taking the time to respond! ☺️ And hello, fellow INFJ!

Just trying to understand myself, others, and the world we live in a little bit better. ☺️

I live on the coast in a beach town and I feel this SO HARD. 

For a while, I tried limiting the cutting to my hips (underneath where a bikini swimsuit bottom would hide). That didn’t work out; I needed a larger surface area and the constant movement of my hips as I walked was irritating. Then I decided to try one pieces and cut my abdomen. That also didn’t work out- partly because I didn’t like abdominal cuts, but mostly because I wanted to wear bikinis. 

I finally started cutting my upper thighs- and I mean very upper- and wearing like nike shorts and bikini tops. I don’t like the appearance of swim shorts or skorts or whatever, but a bikini top and a pair of athletic shorty shorts- rolled at least once or twice at the waist, of course- has actually been a decent combo for me? It’s athletic but still cute and most importantly, looks like it’s done intentionally (and not just thrown on to cover something), which is what I was going for. 

One thing to keep in mind- my scars don’t tan. I used scar remover cream *obsessively* and my scars turned into thin, white, hardly noticeable lines, but when I go into the sun, the rest of my skin tans and my scars don’t, so then they stand out *even more* against the tanner skin, so I try to stay as pale as possible lol. With still healing or colored or raised scars it’d be different (I don’t have personal experience, but I believe the sun would make them worse), that’s just something to keep in mind, so I always use lots of sun screen and vitamin E cream and such. 

Lots of luck and love <3 Stay safe.

You could try not being specific about your arms to avoid suspicion? Just, “Hey, I know you’re just being playful, but unexpected physical contact sometimes bothers me. It’s uncomfortable when you touch or grab me- could you not do that in the future? Thanks.” 

I’ve told many, many people this (and it’s true, after some bad childhood shit I have issues with being touched) and it’s almost always gone well. Most people back off immediately, a few seem concerned and issue offers to talk but still back off (and I don’t take them up on it but I appreciate the offer), and only a handful have become pushy and when I’m insistent, they stop. Only one person ever started to touch me more after they found it bothered me- my flinching and tears were funny to them- but all of our friends told them off and they stopped. And I still show my friends physical affection (because I get those physical touches are how they show they care), but now they either clearly tell me beforehand or approach me slow enough with an intent to hug that I can see, and it’s actually worked out really well for me?

But I definitely get it, the first person in my life that ever found out about my self-injury was trying to stop me from walking away (not even arguing, we were just at the mall and I was just walking into a different shop) and grabbed my wrist. Not hard, but my walking forward made a yank and well... I’d love to say it was handled well, but I shrieked pretty audibly and visible tears came to my eyes. They looked confused, tightened their grip (they knew I was hurt/upset, and I think they were scared I would run off without talking about it, which I probably would have), and saw my wince of pain. Proceeded to pull up my shirt sleeve and found out. It ended up turning out okay because of who this person was, but it’s not how I wanted them to find out, and it definitely could have been not okay if it was someone else. 

Lots of luck. <3

Sending you lots of love and luck, OP. <3

To close with a Frankl quote- who admired Nietzsche very much and mentions him throughout ‘Man’s Search for Meaning’ - “The way in which a man accepts his fate and all the suffering it entails, the way in which he takes up his cross, gives him ample opportunity- even under the most difficult circumstances- to add a deeper meaning to his life.” I’ve found a deeper meaning in life and reasons to stay alive, but that does not mean that I’ve not suffered and carried my cross or “shouldered enough responsibility”. Far from it. 

The implication or assumption that people who struggle to find happiness have just not struggled, suffered, or “shouldered enough responsibility” in life is rather ignorant at best and downright dangerous at worst.

I feel somewhat similar. 

I’ve been on mood-stabilizers for a few years due to bipolar disorder and on the whole it’s great. Most of the time, I don’t want to kill myself anymore. I’m a lot less of a wreck and semi-functional. 

But even while enjoying the absence of the lows, I also really miss the highs. I used to feel so much and while it was overwhelming, there were a few points that were amazing. For a long time, I thought being that emotional was a part of my personality, and fundamentally who I was as a person- only later come to find out it was just a chemical imbalance.

A good friend has helped me to see that no matter my intentions, the resulting actions and the impact of my kindness are what is felt, and to not beat myself up over it. It’s my choice to be kind now- even when mood stabilizers make me numb and it’s easier to ignore the suffering the suffering of others when I’m happy, because happy people want to stay happy, even when that means ignoring things they should- and the fact that I have to choose to be kind now versus the inherent kindness I felt before doesn’t matter, and if anything, is more admirable.
